questions.q: Why does the lesson say responsible AI commitments are called "principles" rather than "rules"?
options: Because AI use cases vary too widely for one universal rule to fit all of them, so principles set direction and governance translates that into fitting controls
Because principles are legally binding and rules are not
Because principles only apply to generative AI, not other machine learning
Because rules are easier to write than principles
questions.explain: Principles are deliberately high-level because a single rule can't fit every AI use case; governance does the work of applying them to a specific system.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six recurring principles the lesson describes?
options: Maximum model size
Fairness
Transparency and explainability
Human oversight
questions.explain: The six are fairness, transparency/explainability, accountability, privacy/security, safety/robustness, and human oversight — not a size target.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does the accountability principle require?
options: A specific person or role owns the system's behavior and outcomes — "the model did it" is not an acceptable answer
Every employee must personally review every model decision
The vendor who built the model is always legally responsible
No AI system can ever be deployed without unanimous board approval
questions.explain: Accountability means a named owner is responsible for the system's behavior, not that everyone or no one is responsible.

questions.q: The lesson connects the fairness principle to which earlier part of this course?
options: The bias controls on training data covered in Chapter 2
The Stripe billing integration
The company's office location policy
The course's quiz-grading system
questions.explain: Fairness is enforced in practice through the bias-in-data controls from Chapter 2, per the lesson's mapping section.

questions.q: Per the lesson, what marks the point where a responsible-AI principle stops being voluntary?
options: When a regulation, contract, or industry standard requires it
When the system passes its first unit test
When the engineering team votes on it
Principles are always voluntary and never become mandatory
questions.explain: Principles become mandatory once law, contract, or standard requires them — the handoff the lesson previews into Lesson 26.
